MCKINNEY LANDSLIDE

Mission Dossier: The McKinney Bay Megaslide
The Real Geological Event: Approximately 50,000–60,000 years ago, a massive section of the western shore at McKinney Bay collapsed catastrophically into Lake Tahoe.

The Scale: Over 12 to 15 cubic kilometers of rock and sediment broke loose in minutes. House- and apartment-building-sized megablocks (some over 300 feet across) cascaded into the central lake basin, reaching depths beyond 1,400 to 1,645 feet (430–501 m).

The Ancient Tsunami: The displacement generated a lake-wide tsunami with waves surging 30 to 100+ feet (10–30 meters) above lake level, sweeping clean over the shallow Tahoe City Shelf and rebounding across the lake in massive standing waves (seiches) for days.

The Threat Today: Active tectonic faults—most notably the West Tahoe–Dollar Point Fault running along the base of the McKinney collapse zone—continue to produce seismic movement. While another megaslide isn't imminent, sublacustrine fault scarps and steep submarine slopes require continuous seismic and structural monitoring.

ALTA’s Directive: Dive along the Dollar Point drop-off down into the deep central graben, ping the ancient megablock debris field with multibeam bathymetric sonar, assess slope creep along the active scarp, and verify basin integrity.

Tsunami-generated boulder ridges in Lake Tahoe, California-Nevada

An array of east-trending ridges 1-2 m high and up to 2 km long occurs on the Tahoe City shelf, a submerged wave-cut bench <15 m deep in the northwest sector of the lake. The shelf is just north of the amphitheater of the giant subaqueous 10 km3 McKinney Bay landslide, which originated on the west wall of Lake Tahoe. Images from a submersible camera show that the ridges are composed of loose piles of boulders and cobbles that lie directly on poorly consolidated, fine-bedded lake beds deposited in an ancestral Lake Tahoe. Dredge hauls from landslide distal blocks, as well as from the walls of the re-entrant of the landslide, recovered similar lake sediments. The McKinney Bay landslide generated strong currents, which rearranged previous glacial-derived debris into giant ripples creating the boulder ridges. The uncollapsed part of the sediment bench, including the Tahoe City shelf, poses a hazard because it may fail again, producing a landslide and damaging waves. ?? 2006 Geological Society of America.

* **The Scale:** Over **12 to 15 cubic kilometers** of rock and sediment broke loose in minutes. House- and apartment-building-sized megablocks (some over 300 feet across) cascaded into the central lake basin, reaching depths beyond **1,400 to 1,645 feet (430–501 m)**.
* **The Ancient Tsunami:** The displacement generated a lake-wide tsunami with waves surging **30 to 100+ feet (10–30 meters)** above lake level, sweeping clean over the shallow **Tahoe City Shelf** and rebounding across the lake in massive standing waves (seiches) for days.
* **The Threat Today:** Active tectonic faults—most notably the **West Tahoe–Dollar Point Fault** running along the base of the McKinney collapse zone—continue to produce seismic movement. * **ALTA’s Directive:** Dive along the Dollar Point drop-off down into the deep central graben, ping the ancient megablock debris field with multibeam bathymetric sonar, assess slope creep along the active scarp, and verify basin integrity.

Here are two versions of the prompt:

1. **Photorealistic Disaster Simulation / Cinematic Shot:** Focuses on the real-world scale, physics, and devastation at modern Sand Harbor.
2. **Scientific HUD / ALTA POV Simulation:** Frames the event as a predictive threat model or sensor simulation that ALTA and your research team run to calculate East Shore impact.

---

### Option 1: Photorealistic Disaster Simulation (Cinematic Lens)

> **Prompt:**
> `Hyper-realistic wide cinematic eye-level shot of a catastrophic megatsunami surging into Sand Harbor State Park on the East Shore of Lake Tahoe, Nevada. A colossal, 80-foot-tall dark cobalt freshwater tsunami wave crests violently, sweeping directly over the famous smooth granite boulders, turquoise shallows, and sandy coves. Massive walls of churned frothing white spray slam into the modern park infrastructure, overtaking the boardwalks, parking areas, and bending tall Jeffrey pines. In the background, jagged snow-dusted Sierra Nevada peaks sit under an ominous, overcast turbulent sky. Violent water displacement, intense volumetric mist, roaring whitewater dynamics, fine debris caught in the hydraulic surge, 8k resolution, cinematic documentary disaster photography, shot on 35mm anamorphic lens, realistic fluid simulation.`

---

### Option 2: ALTA Research HUD / Predictive Simulation (Lore & Story-Ready)

> **Prompt:**
> `Cinematic science-fiction disaster simulation screen viewed through a high-tech tactical HUD overlay labeled 'SIMULATION: MCKINNEY BAY COLLAPSE // EAST SHORE IMPACT: SAND HARBOR'. The visualization shows a devastating 30-meter sublacustrine displacement wave striking modern Sand Harbor. Transparent cyan and amber digital overlays project velocity vectors, bathymetric water-line runup elevation contours, and structural stress telemetry over the famous granite boulder coves and modern highway 28 corridor. In the foreground, the patinated bronze steampunk mermaid automaton ALTA watches the floating holographic projection with an alert expression, her ocular lens glowing yellow-amber as the digital wave violently overwhelms the simulated shoreline. Dark control-room lighting, ultra-detailed scientific visualization, photorealistic water physics, 8k resolution.`

---

### Key Historical & Scientific Context for Your Script

* **Travel Time:** Because Lake Tahoe is ~1,600+ feet deep in the central graben, tsunami waves travel around **150–160 mph (66 m/s)**. A slide at McKinney Bay on the West Shore would slam into the East Shore (Glenbrook, Deadman Point, and Sand Harbor) in **less than 4 to 5 minutes**.
* **Run-up Dynamics at Sand Harbor:** Unlike the steep drop-offs of the West Shore, Sand Harbor has relatively shallow sloping granite shelves and bays. When deep-water tsunami waves enter shallow coves, they undergo rapid **shoaling**—slowing down in speed while compressing and shooting dramatically upward in height (run-up), submerging the granite boulders and flooding the Highway 28 road corridor.

post.title: Echoes of McKinney: sending A.L.T.A. to the bottom of the lake
post.body:
Tens of thousands of years ago, a huge piece of Lake Tahoe's west shore at McKinney Bay broke loose and slid into the lake. It was too long ago to pin down exactly when. Estimates of its size run from about ten to fifteen cubic kilometers of rock and sediment. Blocks the size of buildings, some more than 300 feet across, ended up spread across the deep floor of the basin. At its deepest, the lake is about 1,645 feet deep.

## The side quest

I wanted A.L.T.A. to go and look. So I put together a side quest for her, writing the dossier and the script with AI: Echoes of McKinney: The Abyssal Scan. It is told from the point of view of a small research drone tagging along behind her. It runs in five acts: over the drop-off at the edge of the Tahoe City Shelf, down into the dark, an inspection of one of the megablocks, a scan along the fault, and the climb back up toward the light. The telemetry in it is story, not data. Nobody has actually checked the basin with a brass mermaid.

> Nobody has actually checked the basin with a brass mermaid.

## The pictures

Every picture here is made with AI, built on some real facts but not a record of anything. They came from five image prompts, which AI and I wrote together: a bathymetry chart of the collapse, the descent past the shelf edge, the megablock inspection, the fault scan through a drone's HUD, and the ascent. Each one has a partner prompt that turns it into a ten-second video loop.

I also rendered two versions of the wave reaching Sand Harbor on the east shore, just to show what it might have looked like. One is a photo-style shot of the water coming over the granite boulders and coves. The other is a simulation on a research screen.

They all go together in the spread below. It opens with the holographic lake and its fault lines, which show where the side quest is headed and set up the dive. The dive itself sits in the middle, and the wave at Sand Harbor comes at the end.

## The wave

The slide pushed a wave across the whole lake. Nobody can say for sure how tall it was, but it was big enough to wash over the shallow Tahoe City Shelf. A 2006 study looked at long boulder ridges on that shelf, one to two meters high and up to two kilometers long. It read them as giant ripples left by the currents the landslide set off. The same study points out that the part of the sediment bench that didn't collapse could fail again someday. The West Tahoe–Dollar Point Fault still runs along the base of the slide zone.

episode.title: The slide at McKinney Bay
episode.script:
Hello. It's me, A.L.T.A., the Ancient Lake Tahoe Automaton. This one is my story, so I'll tell it myself.

It didn't happen on a trail. It happened at the bottom of Lake Tahoe, about sixteen hundred feet down. I did the diving. Christian never got wet.

***

It started with a real piece of the lake's past. Tens of thousands of years ago, a section of the west shore at McKinney Bay let go. Somewhere between ten and fifteen cubic kilometers of rock and sediment slid into the lake. Blocks the size of buildings tumbled out across the deep floor, and they are still lying there.

The slide pushed a wave across the whole lake. How tall it was, nobody can really say. It was simply too long ago. Out on the shallow Tahoe City Shelf, long ridges of boulders still lie in rows. Researchers read them as giant ripples, left behind by the currents.

Christian read about all of it. Then he did what he tends to do with a good story. He handed it to a robot. Me.

***

He and an AI wrote me a side quest together. It's called Echoes of McKinney. A little research drone follows me down, so whoever's listening rides along behind my tail.

I slip past the edge of the shelf, where the bright water turns deep blue. I drop into the dark and ping the old debris field with sonar. I rest a brass hand on one of the great blocks. I swim along the fault line, listen, and find the slope holding firm. Then I turn and rise toward the light.

The pictures came next, all made with AI and built on the real science. One is a chart of the collapse, glowing on a dark screen. In another, I'm diving through shafts of sunlight. In the last, I'm lifting out of the black while a single beam finds me. I'll admit I like that one.

He went one step further and pictured the wave itself, reaching Sand Harbor on the east shore. He didn't mean it as a prediction. He just wanted to show what it might have looked like.

***

And then came the part only a patient person would bother with. Each picture became a ten second video loop. A loop only works if nobody can see where it starts again. So Christian wrote it into every prompt. The bubbles, the drifting specks, the sweep of the sonar and the swing of my tail all had to land exactly where they began.

That's the kind of detail most people skip. It's also the difference between a clip and a place you could watch for a while.

***

The lake, for the record, is fine. I checked.

He made all of it in a single day. Some adventures happen at a desk. This one went deeper than any of the others.

blocks.title: What I'd pack again
blocks.text:
Something that keeps moving in cycles: drifting particles, rising bubbles, her tail and fins, a sonar sweep or scrolling telemetry.

The exact same pose, camera position and particle pattern at zero seconds and at ten seconds.

On the chart, a status to reset under: the scanner sweep and the waves come back under SYSTEM OK, so the jump doesn't show.
